problem: Cooperative navigation methods assume unlimited communication every step, and learned communication gates trained with REINFORCE suffer from high variance because the link between a gate decision and episode success is long and noisy. The question of when to spend a limited transmission budget in language-guided navigation is unaddressed.
motivation: Real deployments (search-and-rescue, multi-drone inspection) face hard limits on radio, energy and privacy-constrained disclosure, so message timing matters. The authors examine what a stably trained gate learns and find it contradicts the intuition of communicating when uncertain.
key_idea: Train a lightweight communication gate with BCE on post-hoc 'hindsight' labels (agent wrong while partner right), and show it learns to synchronise GRU hidden states early rather than recover from uncertainty late.
insight: The trained gate fires mostly in steps 0-2 and at slightly higher confidence (0.453 vs 0.413 at B=3), opposite to uncertainty recovery. Alignment analysis shows learned gating (+0.072) approaches always-communicate (+0.078) and beats random (+0.020) and entropy-based (+0.017) gating, and the gain keeps growing after gate firing stops because of GRU propagation. However, navigation SR barely changes, so alignment is only an indirect proxy for benefit.
method: Asymmetric paired task: Agent 0 navigates the full R2R path, Agent 1 starts at the midpoint and navigates the second half, both given the full instruction; each agent has a per-episode budget of B messages.

Navigation backbone: frozen CLIP ViT-B/32 features, CrossModalAttention over language tokens gives context vector c_i(t), a GRU takes [c; partner message; previous action], and candidates are scored by dot product with CLIP candidate features.
Phase 1: pre-train the single-agent policy with teacher-forced imitation learning, without messages.
Phase 2 hindsight labels: roll out without communication and label a step 1 if agent i's action is wrong and the partner's is correct; train a 3-layer MLP gate on (h_i, remaining budget) with BCE.
Inference gating: send c_i(t) when p_send > 0.4 and budget remains, then decrement the budget.
Phase 3: jointly fine-tune both agents with the frozen gate so the policy adapts to received messages.
Analysis: cosine similarity between the two agents' GRU hidden states under learned, random, entropy-based, always and none policies.

setting.backbone: Frozen CLIP ViT-B/32 + CrossModalAttention + GRU navigator + 3-layer MLP gate (trained from scratch)
setting.model_size: hidden dim 512; small model (no parameter count given)
setting.training_data: R2R train episodes only, with no speaker-augmented data, paired asymmetrically as sub-paths
setting.observation: Pre-extracted CLIP ViT-B/32 panoramic features (36 directions x 512), instruction tokens, partner messages, remaining budget
setting.action_space: Discrete nav-graph candidate viewpoints (max 15 candidates, max path length 20)
setting.privileged: Agent 1 has goal-region knowledge by design; hindsight labels use ground-truth actions during training only

numbers.extra: two-agent asymmetric setup; mean of 3 seeds; SR is Agent 0 only
two-agent asymmetric setup; mean of 3 seeds
no communication, single agent, no speaker augmentation

numbers_note: Alignment gains (e.g. +0.072 learned vs +0.020 random at B=3 on val-unseen) are not navigation metrics and are omitted from numbers.
results: Hindsight gating at B=3 gives Agent 0 an SR of 8.9% on val-unseen, matching full communication (8.9%) and slightly above no-comm (8.7%), but below the single-agent 9.2% (the text claims it exceeds it, which the table contradicts). The main result is hidden-state alignment: +0.072 vs +0.020 for random and +0.017 for entropy gating, close to always-communicate (+0.078).
limitations: Absolute navigation is very weak (9.2% val-unseen SR, far below Seq2Seq's 22%), and communication gives negligible SR gains; the two-agent val-seen SR (20.1) is well below the single-agent 43.2.
The alignment proxy may reflect agents becoming similarly wrong; only N=2 agents with fixed asymmetric roles on the discrete R2R graph, with no continuous-environment or real-robot evaluation.
